strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: the optimization tractability of off-policy learning (OPL) objectives in very large action spaces, a practically critical issue for recommender systems where K can reach millions.

Provides a clean conceptual framing that ties optimization difficulty to the effective action-space size K_eff, and correctly observes that MIPS/OffCEM/PC marginalization does not reduce K_eff (since the softmax is still over all K actions), whereas POTEC does—this is a useful unifying insight.

The empirical study is unusually large-scale (MovieLens 60k, Twitch 200k, GoodReads 1M actions) with controlled sweeps over batch size, LR schedule, seeds, noise, logging support, and cluster counts; such scale is rare in the OPL literature and lends credibility.

The cLPI vs cIPS comparison is a genuinely clean test: the authors show cLPI and cIPS share the same greedy oracle decision rule, so differences in learned-policy quality can be attributed more directly to optimization rather than to a different statistical target.
Concavity of the PWLL objective for linear-softmax policies (Proposition 3.1) is correctly derived, and the accompanying convergence guarantees (Appendices C–D) are standard but properly invoked.
Practical, actionable design guidance (objective-aware parametrization, prefer PWLL-style objectives) that is easy to implement and likely to be adopted in practice.
The limitations section is honest about PWLL not being a value estimator, the loss of concavity for deep end-to-end training, and the dependence of PWLL oracles on the logging policy.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('optimization matters more than estimation') is broader than what the evidence supports. The cross-objective comparisons (LPI vs IPS, RegKL vs ES) change both the optimization landscape AND the objective's target policy (LPI oracle ∝ r·π_0 is not the optimal policy, unlike the IPS oracle), so they conflate optimization with statistical target choice. Only the cLPI/cIPS pair isolates optimization cleanly.

The theoretical results (Propositions 2.1 and 2.2) are essentially re-derived from Chen et al. (2019) and Mei et al. (2020a). They are worst-case 'there-exist-instances' statements and do not establish that IPS landscapes are generically hard or how frequently the pathologies occur; the novelty of the optimization theory is therefore limited.

The argument that estimation accuracy does not predict policy quality (Figure 3 vs Figure 2) is confounded: PWLL methods are deliberately excluded from the MSE plot because of their large MSE, so the comparison reduces to a set of IPS-based estimators whose MSEs and rewards are not derived from a controlled variation of estimation error alone.

Key baselines are missing. The direct method (fit a reward model and take argmax) is a standard strong baseline in large action spaces and is not reported; without it, the claim that PWLL beats the best practical alternatives is not fully established.

Main-text evidence rests on small, hard-to-read figures with no numerical tables, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the substantive quantitative support is largely deferred to appendices, making it difficult for a reader to assess effect sizes.

The 'objective-aware parametrization' contribution is intuitive and close to existing ideas (POTEC-style decomposition, reducing K_eff), so its conceptual novelty is modest; it functions more as a practical heuristic than a new principle.

Presentation issues: typographical/notational errors (e.g., 'π^{mtriod}_*'), inconsistent labeling of POTEC/MIPS/OffCEM in some equations, and a somewhat overstated abstract relative to the more careful, narrower claims in the body.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-examined and practically important question—whether optimization difficulty (not estimation accuracy) is the binding constraint in large-action-space OPL—and gives an actionable message for practitioners.

The unified oracle-policy analysis (Section 2.1–2.2 and Appendix B) is a useful synthesis: closed-form maximizers are derived for IPS, cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC and PC, and the observation that POTEC can be read as an optimization strategy for OffCEM with an identical oracle policy is a clean and informative result.

The empirical study is on genuinely large action spaces (MovieLens 60k, Twitch 200k, GoodReads 1M) and is well-structured, with controlled sweeps over batch size, LR schedule, and seeds, plus ablations on cluster count, logging support, reward noise, and reduced K (Appendix E).

The concavity/strong-concavity result for PWLL under linear-softmax policies (Prop. 3.1) and the accompanying SGA convergence rates (Props. D.4–D.5) give a clean optimization rationale, even if the underlying convexity is standard.
The paper is candid about its limitations (PWLL is not a value estimator; concavity only holds for linear-softmax; PWLL oracle depends on π0) and does not overclaim algorithmic novelty.
weaknesses: The theoretical core is derivative: Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are explicitly 'adapted from Chen et al. (2019); Mei et al. (2020a)' and essentially restate known plateau/local-maxima results for softmax-linear-in-π objectives; the only new ingredient is reframing them through K_eff. Likewise, concavity of a positively-weighted softmax log-likelihood (Prop. 3.1) is textbook (multinomial-logit/logistic concavity), so the theoretical contribution is thin for a main-track paper.

The proposed remedy is admitted to be non-novel ('We do not position PWLL as a novel method'); PWLL is reward/advantage-weighted behavioral cloning (Peters 2006; Nair 2020; Wang 2020; Peng 2019). 'Objective-aware parametrization' also reduces to existing practices—restricting the policy to the logging support, and using the POTEC two-stage decomposition, which is itself a prior method. The algorithmic delta is therefore minimal.

The central claim ('optimization matters more than estimation') is not cleanly established. PWLL and IPS-based objectives have different oracle policies/inductive biases, so the higher validation reward of PWLL conflates optimization tractability with inductive-bias alignment to the evaluation metric. This confound is especially concerning here because the logging policy is itself built from the same SVD embeddings/top-k0 construction, making reward-weighted imitation of π0 a strong prior for recovering the hidden items.

The MSE-vs-reward argument (Fig. 3 vs Fig. 2) is essentially a single anecdote (ES vs MIPS) and compares the MSE of a method that is deliberately not a value estimator against that of value estimators, which is not informative. The more relevant test—whether estimation accuracy *among value estimators* predicts learned-policy quality—is not run.

A natural, optimization-friendly baseline is missing: the Direct Method (reward-model argmax) is cited (Jeunen & Goethals) but never included, despite being a standard and highly competitive large-action-space OPL approach. Its absence weakens the claim that the observed gap is specifically about optimization of IPS objectives rather than about model-based vs. importance-weighted learning.

The theory-to-experiment mapping is loose: the propositions are for a single-context linear-softmax policy, whereas the experiments use multi-context inner-product policies with a fixed context embedding and learned action embeddings or a projection. The paper never establishes that the predicted O(K_eff) plateaus/exponential local maxima are what the experiments actually exhibit.

Presentation/carelessness issues undermine confidence: garbled symbols (e.g., 'π^{mtriod}', 's_{θ_θ}', a broken Proposition 3.1 statement), and duplicated/incorrect reference entries (e.g., Saito and Joachims appearing as both 2022 and 2023; multiple Sakhi entries with mismatched years).

strengths: Provides a clear and timely diagnosis of optimization pathologies in off-policy learning for large action spaces, with theoretical results showing plateaus and many local maxima scale with the effective action space size.
Introduces and validates objective-aware policy parametrization, a simple but effective principle that aligns policy structure with the oracle structure of IPS-based objectives to reduce K_eff.

Empirically demonstrates on three large-scale recommendation datasets (60k, 200k, 1M actions) that PWLL objectives are far more robust to optimization hyperparameters and often outperform sophisticated IPS-based methods.
The paper is well-written, with clear exposition of the oracle policies for a wide range of IPS-based estimators and a helpful taxonomy of PWLL variants.
Extensive ablations (seeds, reward noise, cluster sensitivity, logging support, pessimism, smaller action spaces) strengthen the empirical claims and practical guidance.
Limitations are honestly discussed, including PWLL's unsuitability for OPE, the linear-softmax concavity assumption, and the dependence of oracle policies on the logging policy.
Code and artifacts are stated to be publicly available, and implementation details are largely provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical optimization results (Propositions 2.1 and 2.2) are adapted from existing work and are existence/worst-case results; they do not prove that the specific empirical settings necessarily suffer from these pathologies, nor do they provide matching lower bounds for the algorithms studied.

The central claim that 'optimization matters more than estimation' is somewhat overgeneralized from the chosen datasets and experimental protocol; the comparison between PWLL and IPS-based objectives conflates optimization landscape with differences in statistical target and inductive bias.

The evaluation protocol for 'validation reward' and the computation of MSE are not fully specified in the main text or appendix, making it difficult to assess exactly how policies are compared and what ground truth is used for the MSE plots.

The MSE comparison involving PWLL objectives is not meaningful because PWLL is explicitly not a value estimator; including it in an MSE figure (even if excluded from the plot) could mislead readers about the role of estimation accuracy.
The concavity guarantee for PWLL holds only for linear-softmax policies; for end-to-end deep policies, the paper relies on informal gradient-structure arguments rather than formal guarantees.

The objective-aware parametrization for IPS/cIPS/ES restricts to the logging support S_0, which is safe for the objective's oracle but may lose true optimal actions if the logging policy has poor coverage; the paper acknowledges this but the practical trade-off is not quantified.

No new algorithm is proposed; the main contribution is a diagnostic and empirical study, which is useful but may be seen as incremental relative to existing work on IPS, MIPS, POTEC, and weighted behavioral cloning.
